$comment: Root ADR-0619. The base of the AWS account the data jobs move to (root ADR-0616): which account, which region, the tags every resource carries, the state bucket, the account's monthly budget, the network, and Dagster's place: its cluster, service, database and alarm (root ADR-0616 A1). infra/aws reads this file for the account, the names, the sizes and where its images come from (it also reads the version contract and the host's SQL files, and keeps mechanical constants such as ports and timings in its .tf files); the provider refuses every other account (allowed_account_ids), so an apply under the wrong profile stops before it reads or changes anything. Applied from the laptop with the SSO profile after the PR merges (docs/runbooks/aws-platform.md); nothing applies it on the data host.

account.name: perfectory-platform-prod
account.reason: The organization's platform account (made 2026-11-09 for the Seoul front door, root ADR-0461). The management account and the old gongzzang production account are never targets: they are not listed here, so the provider refuses them.

images.reason: Where the images AWS runs come from (root ADR-0619 §7, ADR-0620, ADR-0616 §2-4): the release package on GHCR, by digest. The release workflow's aws-images job writes one record per commit (aws-images.json: every image's digest), attests it with the images and publishes it under record_tag. An apply takes one commit: scripts/deploy/aws-release-images.py reads its record and verifies the record and every image it names against this repository, this workflow, this ref and that commit (gh attestation verify) before it writes a digest; infra/aws refuses an image outside this repository. mirrors: images of the version contract (tools/technology-versions.contract.json container_images) that AWS runs although we do not build them, psql's postgres; the same job copies each by its pinned digest into this repository (skopeo --all --preserve-digests, under mirror_tag), so a task pulls it from here by the same digest and never from Docker Hub (root ADR-0619 §7).

state.reason: The state of an AWS stack lives in its own account: the SSO role that applies it reads and writes it, so no second credential (the R2 keys the host's stacks use) reaches the laptop. Versioned so an apply that went wrong can be rolled back to the earlier state; old versions leave after 90 days. Locked by the S3 backend's own lock file (use_lockfile). The state holds no secret: the master password is RDS's own (manage_master_user_password) and the Dagster role's is written write-only (secret_string_wo); the state holds only the secrets' ARNs.

budget.name: perfectory-platform-monthly
budget.reason: Owner approval 2026-11-25: collection on AWS at about 92 USD a month on ARM, 160 in a month with a bulk collection (root ADR-0616 §10, re-stated at Fargate ARM prices); the owner raised the limit to 200 on 2026-11-27. Actual spend past 100 is the first notice, past 200 the second; a forecast past 200 tells before the month ends. The budget mails the account's own registered address (a variable at apply time, never committed: this repository is public); budget mail needs no confirmation. Budgets without actions cost nothing.

network.address_reason: The VPC's own address block is given at apply time (TF_VAR_vpc_cidr), not written here: this repository is public and holds no private network addressing (scripts/guard/public-repository-safety.sh). This file decides the shape: a /16 cut into /20 subnets, each subnet the netnum its zone has in public_subnets or private_subnets (cidrsubnet). Once the VPC exists the runbook reads its block back from AWS, and the VPC and its subnets refuse to be destroyed (prevent_destroy), so a wrong block stops the plan instead of replacing the network.
network.reason: No NAT gateway and no load balancer (root ADR-0616 §1, §10). Tasks run in the public subnets with a public IPv4 address and no inbound rule: they reach the sources, R2, GHCR and the AWS APIs through the internet gateway. The private subnets have no route out and hold only the database (RDS needs subnets in two zones). Two zones, because RDS requires them; 2a and 2c because every Fargate and RDS class is offered there. The account's default VPC is left as it is and used by nothing here.

ecs.reason: One cluster for the Dagster service and every run task it launches (root ADR-0616 §1-§2). Container Insights stays off: the alarm reads the service metrics ECS publishes for free. Every role a run task may carry (the default run role with no policy, the run execution role, each lane's role) is under run_role_path, and Dagster may pass a role under that path and no other.

dagster.services_reason: The webserver and the daemon are each their own always-on service (coordinator 2026-11-27; Dagster's Docker and Helm deployments run them apart): one can be sized, restarted and deployed without the other, and a webserver that dies no longer stops the daemon (both containers of the one task were essential). Any number of webservers may run, so its deploy starts the new task before it stops the old one; a deployment has a single daemon, so its deploy stops the old one first (Dagster 1.13 docs, deploying-dagster-as-a-service). Each is Fargate's smallest ARM size, 0.25 vCPU and 0.5 GB, by root ADR-0574's rule (limit >= 1.5 x measured peak). Measured 2026-11-27 on AWS in the one task they shared (9.3 h, ECS task stats, ECS Exec): daemon 0.085 vCPU over 180 s, peak 263.6 MiB; webserver 0.018 vCPU, peak 246.7 MiB; the task's per-minute CloudWatch average 0.15 vCPU (p99 0.17), 301-303 MiB. On ai-server with 71 jobs (cAdvisor since 2026-11-25): daemon peak 299 MiB, 0.15 cores median and 0.25 at most (i5-13600KF); webserver 287 MiB, 0.02 cores. Both peaks x 1.5 fit 512 MiB. The daemon's CPU grows with the sensors and automation conditions the lanes bring: measure it again as lanes move in, and raise its size here. At root ADR-0616 §10's Seoul prices each is 6.8 + 1.5 USD a month and 3.65 for its public IPv4.
dagster.code_locations_reason: One ECS service per code location (coordinator 2026-11-26, the layout of Dagster's ECS deployment guide): a gRPC code server from the location's image, reached by the webserver and the daemon as <location>.<namespace> (Cloud Map private DNS) on its port, listed in orchestration/dagster/aws/workspace.yaml. 0.25 vCPU and 0.5 GB on Fargate ARM, Fargate's smallest, by root ADR-0574's rule: the one location's server peaked at 242 MiB (CloudWatch, 2026-11-26..27; 204 MiB steady) and 0.05 vCPU on average, so 1.5 x its peak is 363 MiB. A reload holds a second code process until the first stops (dagster code-server). The location grows as lanes move in (on ai-server the code process of 71 jobs is 209 MiB, the proxy about 100): measure it again then and raise its size here. About 6.8 + 1.5 USD a month, 3.65 for its public IPv4, 0.10 for its Cloud Map instance and 0.5 for the namespace's hosted zone (Seoul prices, root ADR-0616 §10). The webserver and the daemon run the Dagster image (Dockerfile.aws-dagster), which holds no location's code.
dagster.reason: Owner approval 2026-11-25 (root ADR-0616 A1): Dagster always on, on Fargate ARM; first the webserver and the daemon in one task of 0.5 vCPU and 2 GB, since 2026-11-27 each its own service (services). Their image is the release's Dagster image by digest (root ADR-0620), given at apply time; the workspace is the AWS code locations, which hold no job until A2 moves collectors one at a time. Runs are tasks of their own (EcsRunLauncher), sized per run. No inbound rule and no public address of its own beyond the task's IPv4 for egress; the UI is reached by SSM port forwarding (ECS Exec). EcsRunLauncher registers every run's task definition in the family <run_task_definition_prefix>_<hashes> (dagster-aws get_task_definition_family; dagster-aws 0.29.27 refuses a prefix over 16 characters when it builds the launcher), and Dagster's role may start only that family: never the database bootstrap, which carries the master user's secret.

database.one_off_wait_reason: How long an apply waits for one one-off task (the bootstrap, or the migrate task) to stop before it fails (infra/aws/pre-deploy.sh). It bounds the applier's wait only: a task past it keeps running, and the next apply waits for the migrator's lock (sqlx). Not measured on RDS; the data host runs the same migrations inside its deploy.
database.name: dagster

foundation.name: foundation
foundation.reason: The Bronze ledger's place (root ADR-0616 A1b, coordinator 2026-11-26): the data host's foundation schema on this instance, made by the same sqlx migrations (foundation-migrate from the release's arm64 runtime image), empty until a collector moves in (A2). The role names are the ones the migrations and infra/compose/grant-foundation-runtime.sql name (the runtime role is the one the collectors connect as on the data host). The migrator owns the schema; the runtime role reads and writes rows; each has its own secret, written write-only. Every rollout runs bootstrap, migrate, grants and finalize before the service moves (infra/aws/pre-deploy.sh).

database.reason: Dagster's storage (runs, events, schedules; 1,001 MB on ai-server) on RDS PostgreSQL, one zone, the smallest Graviton class (root ADR-0616 §1, §10: 18.25 USD a month plus 0.131 a GB). The disk grows by itself up to max_allocated_storage_gb (RDS storage autoscaling, no cost until it grows; at the ceiling 13.1 USD a month): on ai-server the ledger's schema `catalog` is 527 MB and Dagster's storage 1,001 MB (measured 2026-11-26). In the private subnets only, reached from the tasks' security group only, TLS required (PostgreSQL 15+ on RDS forces SSL by default). Least privilege: Dagster and every run task connect as app_username, a role that owns only this database, with its own secret (app_secret, in the shape Secrets Manager's RDS rotation reads; the password is written write-only, never in the state). The master user (master_username, its password RDS's own in Secrets Manager) is read only by the one-off bootstrap task that creates that role (infra/aws/database-bootstrap.sql). The Bronze ledger has its own database on this instance (foundation). Deletion protection and a final snapshot, so neither an apply nor a mistaken delete removes it.

not_running.reason: A Dagster service's not-running alarm fires only after window_minutes one-minute periods in a row in which ECS published no CPU sample of the service (one a minute while a task runs, none while no task runs, which counts as breaching): M of N is window_minutes of window_minutes. The window is longer than the longest stop a deploy makes: on 2026-11-27 (the apply of #1770) the old daemon service took 86 s to stop and its new task ran 56 s later, 2 min 22 s without a task, and a daemon deploy always stops its old task before it starts the new one (dagster.services_reason). So a gap of up to nine minutes is no alarm and ten minutes is. A brand-new service has no sample before its first task and goes to ALARM once, until that task runs.

alarms.ok_reason: An alarm's own OK action fires on every move into OK, also out of INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which every new or changed alarm starts in: on 2026-11-27 the six near-limit alarms of #1771 each sent an OK on creation. So no alarm has OK actions; one EventBridge rule on CloudWatch's alarm state change events (detail.previousState.value ALARM, detail.state.value OK) sends the OK, as a Chatbot custom notification with the alarm's name and time only, because Chatbot does not render alarm events that come from EventBridge rules (Amazon Q Developer in chat applications admin guide, related services).

near_limit.reason: Root ADR-0574 §5 on AWS (coordinator 2026-11-27): a service near its task size is named before it dies or starves. Every always-on service (dagster.services and every code location) has two alarms on the ECS service metrics, which are free and, with one container per task, that container's own: memory (MemoryUtilization, the minute's maximum, which leaves out reclaimable cache) above memory_percent of the task's memory, and CPU (CPUUtilization, average) above cpu_percent of its vCPU, each for 15 minutes. Memory is the host's FoundationContainerMemoryNearCap (90 % for 15 minutes): on ai-server foundation-api sat at its cap for two weeks and was killed 69 times (root ADR-0573), and the daemon's working set stood at 379 of its 384 MiB on 2026-11-19. CPU is lower because Fargate throttles at the task's vCPU instead of killing: a daemon past it runs its ticks late and nothing fails, so 80 % sustained is the warning. On 2026-11-27 the daemon used 34 % of its 0.25 vCPU and its memory peaked at 52 % (264 of 512 MiB). The fix is a measured size in this contract (dagster.services, dagster.code_locations).

chatbot.reason: AWS Chatbot (Amazon Q Developer in chat applications) has its control plane in four Regions (us-east-2, us-west-2, ap-southeast-1, eu-west-1), none of them ap-northeast-2, and its console in us-east-2 only. The channel configuration is managed through us-east-2; the topic and the alarms stay in the account's Region (one configuration takes topics of any Region). The service stores its configurations in those four Regions and may process a notification in any of them.

alarms.reason: Every alarm of this account publishes to one SNS topic. Urgent alarms go to Slack (owner, 2026-11-20) through AWS Chatbot (owner, 2026-11-26): the topic is bound to one Slack channel and no token or webhook is stored. Which alarms reach Slack is which alarms publish to the topic, in code (first: Dagster not running). The owner authorizes the Slack workspace once in the console; the workspace and channel ids are apply-time variables, not in this public repository.
